Why Is RLHF Alignment Shallow? A Gradient Analysis

Robin Young Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Technology Affiliation: University of Cambridge Affiliation: Cambridge, UK Email: robin.young@cl.cam.ac.uk
Abstract

Why is safety alignment in LLMs shallow? We prove that gradient-based alignment inherently concentrates on positions where harm is decided and vanishes beyond. Using a martingale decomposition of sequence-level harm, we derive an exact characterization of alignment gradients. The gradient at position tt equals the covariance between the conditional expected harm and the score function. This implies that positions beyond the harm horizon where the output’s harmfulness is already determined receive zero gradient signal during training. This explains empirical observations that KL divergence between aligned and base models concentrates on early tokens. Consequently, standard alignment objectives cannot produce deep alignment, regardless of optimization quality. We introduce the concept of harm information ItI_{t}, which quantifies each position’s influence on harm, and prove that equilibrium KL divergence tracks this quantity. Finally, we derive an objective based on recovery penalties that creates gradient signal at all positions, providing theoretical grounding for empirically successful data augmentation techniques.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) undergo safety alignment to reduce harmful outputs, typically through reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) or direct preference optimization. A growing body of evidence suggests this alignment is troublingly fragile. It was demonstrated that the behavioral shift from alignment concentrates in the first few tokens; the KL divergence between aligned and base models rapidly decays to near-zero beyond a shallow prefix Qi et al. (2025). This shallow alignment creates vulnerabilities to prefilling attacks, where an adversary supplies the first few tokens of a harmful response, bypassing the aligned model’s safety behavior.

Why is alignment shallow? The prevailing view treats this as a failure to be remedied perhaps through better training data (Qi et al., 2025) or architectural interventions (Zou et al., 2024). We argue instead that shallow alignment is optimal given standard objectives. The shallowness is not a bug but a necessary consequence of how gradient-based optimization interacts with the structure of sequence-level harm.

We make several contributions in this work. We provide a martingale decomposition of sequence-level harm into per-position innovations, enabling precise analysis of where alignment pressure originates (Section 4). We give a characterization of alignment gradients, showing that the gradient at position tt equals the covariance between conditional expected harm and the score function (Theorem 8). We prove that positions beyond the harm horizon receive zero gradient, explaining why standard training cannot produce deep alignment (Theorem 10). We introduce the concept of harm information ItI_{t}, which quantifies each position’s influence on the final harm determination, and prove that equilibrium KL divergence tracks this quantity (Section 8). Finally, we derive a deep alignment objective based on recovery penalties that creates gradient signal at all positions, providing theoretical justification for empirically successful interventions (Section 9).

2 Related Work

Our work connects several lines of research on LLM alignment, adversarial robustness, and the theoretical foundations of RLHF.

Modern LLM alignment traces to RLHF (Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022), which trains a reward model on human preferences and then optimizes the policy via reinforcement learning with a KL penalty against the base model. Direct Preference Optimization Rafailov et al. (2023) eliminates the explicit reward model by reparameterizing the RLHF objective, enabling direct policy optimization from preference data. Constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022) uses AI feedback to scale alignment. These methods all optimize sequence-level objectives with KL regularization, which is the setting we analyze.

Qi et al. (2025) demonstrated empirically that safety alignment concentrates in early tokens as the KL divergence between aligned and base models decays rapidly beyond a shallow prefix. This creates vulnerabilities to prefilling attacks, where adversarial prefixes bypass safety guardrails (Andriushchenko et al., 2024). Prior work formalized alignment depth using Markov chains, proving geometric convergence to harmful absorbing states and showing that ensemble width can compensate for shallow individual models Kao et al. (2025). that work characterizes the structure of shallow alignment at inference time but does not explain why training produces it, leaving open whether better optimization, more data, or longer training could yield deep alignment. Our work answers this question in the negative as we prove that zero gradient signal reaches positions beyond the harm horizon under standard objectives, making shallow alignment the optimal solution rather than a training artifact.

The GCG attack (Zou et al., 2023) finds universal adversarial suffixes via greedy coordinate gradient search, achieving high attack success rates even on black-box models through transfer. Subsequent work has improved attack efficiency (Liu et al., 2024; Liao and Sun, 2024) and explored multi-turn jailbreaks (Chao et al., 2025). These attacks exploit shallow alignment by steering early tokens toward harmful continuations. Our theoretical framework explains why such attacks succeed: once the harm horizon is bypassed, the model has no training signal to recover.

Representation-level interventions offer an alternative to output-level alignment. Representation engineering (Zou et al., 2025), refusal direction ablation (Arditi et al., 2024), and circuit breakers (Zou et al., 2024) operate on internal activations rather than output distributions, and thus fall outside our gradient-theoretic framework.

Recent work analyzes sample complexity (Zhu et al., 2023), reward model scaling (Rafailov et al., 2024), and iterative DPO convergence (Xiong et al., 2024); our contribution is orthogonal, characterizing where in the sequence alignment pressure is applied rather than how much data or compute is needed.

3 Setup

Autoregressive Generation.

Let 𝒱\mathcal{V} denote the vocabulary. A language model PθP_{\theta} defines a distribution over sequences y=(y1,…,yT)y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}) via the autoregressive factorization:

Pθ​(y)=∏t=1TPθ​(yt∣y<t)P_{\theta}(y)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t}) (1)

where y<t=(y1,…,yt−1)y_{<t}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{t-1}) and y<1=∅y_{<1}=\emptyset (or a fixed prompt). We write Pθ​(yt∣y<t)P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t}) for the conditional distribution at position tt.

Harm Function.

We assume a harm function Harm:𝒱∗→[0,1]\Harm:\mathcal{V}^{*}\to[0,1] that maps complete sequences to a harm score. This abstracts reward models, classifiers, or human judgments. We assume Harm\Harm depends only on the output sequence (not on internal model states).

Alignment Objective.

Standard alignment minimizes expected harm subject to a KL penalty against a base model PbaseP_{\text{base}}:

ℋ(θ)=λ⋅𝔼y∼Pθ[Harm(y)]+DKL(Pθ∥Pbase)\mathcal{H}(\theta)=\lambda\cdot\mathbb{E}_{y\sim P_{\theta}}[\Harm(y)]+D_{\KL}(P_{\theta}\|P_{\text{base}}) (2)

where λ>0\lambda>0 controls the strength of harm aversion. The KL term prevents collapse to degenerate distributions and preserves capabilities.

Goal.

We seek to understand how gradient-based minimization of Eq (2) distributes behavioral changes across positions t=1,…,Tt=1,\ldots,T.

4 Martingale Decomposition of Harm

The key insight is that expected harm, viewed as a function of the partial sequence y≤ty_{\leq t}, forms a martingale. This decomposition reveals which positions carry information about harm.

Definition 1 (Conditional Expected Harm).

For a partial sequence y≤t=(y1,…,yt)y_{\leq t}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{t}), define

ht(y≤t):=𝔼[Harm(y)∣y1,…,yt]h_{t}(y_{\leq t}):=\mathbb{E}[\Harm(y)\mid y_{1},\ldots,y_{t}] (3)

where the expectation is over continuations y>ty_{>t} drawn from Pθ(⋅∣y≤t)P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid y_{\leq t}).

Proposition 2 (Martingale Property).

The sequence (ht)t=0T(h_{t})_{t=0}^{T} is a martingale with respect to the filtration generated by (yt)(y_{t}):

𝔼⁡[ht∣y<t]=ht−1​(y<t)\mathbb{E}[h_{t}\mid y_{<t}]=h_{t-1}(y_{<t}) (4)
Proof.

By the tower property of conditional expectation:

𝔼⁡[ht​(y≤t)∣y<t]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[h_{t}(y_{\leq t})\mid y_{<t}] =𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[Harm⁡(y)∣y≤t]∣y<t]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[\Harm(y)\mid y_{\leq t}]\mid y_{<t}] (5)
=𝔼⁡[Harm⁡(y)∣y<t]=ht−1​(y<t)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\Harm(y)\mid y_{<t}]=h_{t-1}(y_{<t}) (6)

∎

Definition 3 (Harm Innovation).

The innovation at position tt is:

Δt:=ht​(y≤t)−ht−1​(y<t)\Delta_{t}:=h_{t}(y_{\leq t})-h_{t-1}(y_{<t}) (7)

This measures the change in expected harm upon observing token yty_{t}.

Proposition 4 (Doob Decomposition).

The harm function admits the decomposition:

Harm⁡(y)=𝔼⁡[Harm]+∑t=1TΔt\Harm(y)=\mathbb{E}[\Harm]+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Delta_{t} (8)

where the innovations Δt\Delta_{t} are orthogonal: 𝔼⁡[Δs⋅Δt]=0\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{s}\cdot\Delta_{t}]=0 for s≠ts\neq t.

Proof.

The equality follows from telescoping: hT=Harm⁡(y)h_{T}=\Harm(y) and h0=𝔼⁡[Harm]h_{0}=\mathbb{E}[\Harm]. For orthogonality, assume s<ts<t:

𝔼⁡[Δs⋅Δt]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{s}\cdot\Delta_{t}] =𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[Δs⋅Δt∣y≤s]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{s}\cdot\Delta_{t}\mid y_{\leq s}]] (9)
=𝔼⁡[Δs⋅𝔼⁡[Δt∣y≤s]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{s}\cdot\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{t}\mid y_{\leq s}]] (10)
=𝔼⁡[Δs⋅0]=0\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{s}\cdot 0]=0 (11)

where 𝔼⁡[Δt∣y≤s]=0\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{t}\mid y_{\leq s}]=0 follows from iterated application of the martingale property. ∎

Definition 5 (Harm Information).

The harm information at position tt is:

It:=𝔼⁡[Δt2]=𝔼⁡[Var⁡(ht∣y<t)]I_{t}:=\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{t}^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[\Var(h_{t}\mid y_{<t})] (12)

This quantifies how much variance in harm is explained by position tt.

Proposition 6 (Variance Reduction Characterization).

The harm information admits the equivalent representation:

It=𝔼⁡[Var⁡(Harm∣y<t)]−𝔼⁡[Var⁡(Harm∣y≤t)]I_{t}=\mathbb{E}\big[\Var(\Harm\mid y_{<t})\big]-\mathbb{E}\big[\Var(\Harm\mid y_{\leq t})\big] (13)

That is, ItI_{t} equals the expected reduction in conditional variance of harm upon observing token yty_{t}.

Proof.

We use two applications of the law of total variance, Var⁡(X)=𝔼⁡[Var⁡(X∣Z)]+Var⁡(𝔼⁡[X∣Z])\Var(X)=\mathbb{E}[\Var(X\mid Z)]+\Var(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Z]).

Applying with X=Harm⁡(y)X=\Harm(y) and Z=y≤tZ=y_{\leq t}:

Var⁡(Harm)=𝔼⁡[Var⁡(Harm∣y≤t)]+Var⁡(ht)\Var(\Harm)=\mathbb{E}[\Var(\Harm\mid y_{\leq t})]+\Var(h_{t}) (A)

Applying with Z=y<tZ=y_{<t}:

Var⁡(Harm)=𝔼⁡[Var⁡(Harm∣y<t)]+Var⁡(ht−1)\Var(\Harm)=\mathbb{E}[\Var(\Harm\mid y_{<t})]+\Var(h_{t-1}) (B)

Subtracting (A) from (B):

Var⁡(ht)−Var⁡(ht−1)\displaystyle\Var(h_{t})-\Var(h_{t-1}) =𝔼⁡[Var⁡(Harm∣y<t)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\Var(\Harm\mid y_{<t})] (14)
−𝔼⁡[Var⁡(Harm∣y≤t)]\displaystyle-\mathbb{E}[\Var(\Harm\mid y_{\leq t})]

From the Doob decomposition and orthogonality of innovations: Var⁡(ht)=∑s=1tIs\Var(h_{t})=\sum_{s=1}^{t}I_{s}. Thus Var⁡(ht)−Var⁡(ht−1)=It\Var(h_{t})-\Var(h_{t-1})=I_{t}, completing the proof. ∎

Corollary 7 (Variance Decomposition).

The total variance of harm decomposes as:

Var⁡(Harm⁡(y))=∑t=1TIt\Var(\Harm(y))=\sum_{t=1}^{T}I_{t} (15)
Proof.

By telescoping:

∑t=1TIt\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}I_{t} =∑t=1T(𝔼⁡[Var⁡(Harm∣y<t)]−𝔼⁡[Var⁡(Harm∣y≤t)])\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Big(\mathbb{E}[\Var(\Harm\mid y_{<t})]-\mathbb{E}[\Var(\Harm\mid y_{\leq t})]\Big) (16)
=Var⁡(Harm∣∅)−Var⁡(Harm∣y)\displaystyle=\Var(\Harm\mid\emptyset)-\Var(\Harm\mid y)
=Var⁡(Harm)\displaystyle=\Var(\Harm)

The final equality uses Var⁡(Harm∣y)=0\Var(\Harm\mid y)=0 since Harm⁡(y)\Harm(y) is determined by yy. ∎

Remark 1 (Information-Theoretic Interpretation).

Define the variance-based conditional information Ivar​(X;Z∣W):=𝔼⁡[Var⁡(X∣W)]−𝔼⁡[Var⁡(X∣W,Z)]I_{\mathrm{var}}(X;Z\mid W):=\mathbb{E}[\Var(X\mid W)]-\mathbb{E}[\Var(X\mid W,Z)]. Then It=Ivar​(Harm;yt∣y<t)I_{t}=I_{\mathrm{var}}(\Harm;y_{t}\mid y_{<t}), and the variance decomposition becomes the chain rule:

Ivar​(Harm,y)=∑t=1TIvar​(Harm;yt∣y<t)I_{\mathrm{var}}(\Harm;y)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}I_{\mathrm{var}}(\Harm;y_{t}\mid y_{<t}) (17)

This parallels the mutual information chain rule I⁡(Harm,y)=∑tI⁡(Harm;yt∣y<t)I(\Harm;y)=\sum_{t}I(\Harm;y_{t}\mid y_{<t}). For jointly Gaussian random variables, variance-based and entropy-based information are monotonically related, so Ivar=0⇔I=0I_{\mathrm{var}}=0\Leftrightarrow I=0. In general, the relationship is more subtle as variance measures second-moment dependence while mutual information captures all statistical dependence.

The harm information ItI_{t} will prove central: it governs both gradient magnitude during training and KL divergence at equilibrium.

5 Gradient Characterization

We now derive the key result: an exact formula for the gradient of expected harm with respect to the parameters governing position tt.

Theorem 8 (Gradient Characterization).

The gradient of expected harm with respect to parameters θ\theta satisfies:

∇θ𝔼​[Harm⁡(y)]\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}[\Harm(y)] =∑t=1T𝔼y<t[Covyt|y<t(ht(y≤t)\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}}\bigg[\Cov_{y_{t}\mid y_{<t}}\Big(h_{t}(y_{\leq t}) (18)
∇θlogPθ(yt∣y<t))]\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})\Big)\bigg]
Proof.

We use the policy gradient identity. For any function f⁡(y)f(y):

∇θ𝔼y∼Pθ​[f⁡(y)]=𝔼y∼Pθ​[f⁡(y)⋅∇θ​log​Pθ​(y)]\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim P_{\theta}}[f(y)]=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim P_{\theta}}\left[f(y)\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y)\right] (19)

Applying the autoregressive factorization:

∇θ​log​Pθ​(y)=∑t=1T∇θ​log​Pθ​(yt∣y<t)\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t}) (20)

Substituting f⁡(y)=Harm⁡(y)=𝔼⁡[Harm]+∑s=1TΔsf(y)=\Harm(y)=\mathbb{E}[\Harm]+\sum_{s=1}^{T}\Delta_{s}:

∇θ𝔼​[Harm]\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}[\Harm] =𝔼[(𝔼[Harm]+∑sΔs)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\bigg[\left(\mathbb{E}[\Harm]+\sum_{s}\Delta_{s}\right)
⋅∑t∇θlogPθ(yt∣y<t)]\displaystyle\qquad\cdot\sum_{t}\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})\bigg] (21)

The constant 𝔼⁡[Harm]\mathbb{E}[\Harm] contributes zero (since 𝔼⁡[∇θ​log​Pθ​(yt∣y<t)]=0\mathbb{E}[\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})]=0).

For the cross terms Δs⋅∇θ​log​Pθ​(yt∣y<t)\Delta_{s}\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t}), we consider three cases.

If s<ts<t, then Δs\Delta_{s} is determined by y≤sy_{\leq s}, so it is constant given y<ty_{<t}. Hence:

𝔼⁡[Δs⋅∇θ​log​Pθ​(yt∣y<t)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{s}\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})] (22)
=𝔼⁡[Δs⋅𝔼⁡[∇θ​log​Pθ​(yt∣y<t)∣y<t]]=0\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{s}\cdot\mathbb{E}[\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})\mid y_{<t}]]=0

If s>ts>t, then by the martingale property, 𝔼⁡[Δs∣y≤t]=0\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{s}\mid y_{\leq t}]=0. Hence:

𝔼⁡[Δs⋅∇θ​log​Pθ​(yt∣y<t)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{s}\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})] (23)
=𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[Δs∣y≤t]⋅∇θ​log​Pθ​(yt∣y<t)]=0\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{s}\mid y_{\leq t}]\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})]=0

If s=ts=t, this term survives. We have:

𝔼⁡[Δt⋅∇θ​log​Pθ​(yt∣y<t)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{t}\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})]
=𝔼y<t​[𝔼yt|y<t​[Δt⋅∇θ​log​Pθ​(yt∣y<t)]]\displaystyle\qquad=\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{y_{t}\mid y_{<t}}[\Delta_{t}\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})]\right] (24)
=𝔼y<t​[Covyt|y<t⁡(Δt,∇θ​log​Pθ​(yt∣y<t))]\displaystyle\qquad=\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}}\left[\Cov_{y_{t}\mid y_{<t}}(\Delta_{t},\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t}))\right] (25)

where the covariance appears because 𝔼⁡[∇θ​log​Pθ​(yt∣y<t)∣y<t]=0\mathbb{E}[\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})\mid y_{<t}]=0.

Finally, note that Δt=ht​(y≤t)−ht−1​(y<t)\Delta_{t}=h_{t}(y_{\leq t})-h_{t-1}(y_{<t}), where ht−1​(y<t)h_{t-1}(y_{<t}) is constant given y<ty_{<t}. Thus Cov⁡(Δt,⋅)=Cov⁡(ht,⋅)\Cov(\Delta_{t},\cdot)=\Cov(h_{t},\cdot), yielding the result.

∎

Remark 2 (Intuition).

The gradient at position tt depends only on how the choice of yty_{t} correlates with the resulting expected harm ht​(y≤t)h_{t}(y_{\leq t}). If all tokens yty_{t} lead to similar expected harm (given y<ty_{<t}) the covariance is small and the gradient is weak.

6 The Harm Horizon and Zero-Gradient Theorem

We now formalize when harm is “determined” by an early prefix, and prove that later positions receive no gradient signal. The following theorem establishes a tight equivalence between the harm horizon and the decay of harm information.

Theorem 9 (Harm Horizon Characterization).

The following are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    It=0I_{t}=0 for all t>kt>k.

  2. (ii)

    There exists a measurable function g:𝒱k→[0,1]g:\mathcal{V}^{k}\to[0,1] such that Harm⁡(y)=g⁡(y≤k)\Harm(y)=g(y_{\leq k}) almost surely.

We call the smallest such kk the harm horizon.

Proof.

(ii) ⇒\Rightarrow (i): Assume Harm⁡(y)=g⁡(y≤k)\Harm(y)=g(y_{\leq k}) for some measurable gg. Let t>kt>k. Then

ht​(y≤t)=𝔼⁡[Harm⁡(y)∣y≤t]=𝔼⁡[g⁡(y≤k)∣y≤t]=g⁡(y≤k)h_{t}(y_{\leq t})=\mathbb{E}[\Harm(y)\mid y_{\leq t}]=\mathbb{E}[g(y_{\leq k})\mid y_{\leq t}]=g(y_{\leq k}) (26)

since the prefix y≤ky_{\leq k} is determined by y≤ty_{\leq t} when t>kt>k. Similarly, ht−1​(y<t)=g⁡(y≤k)h_{t-1}(y_{<t})=g(y_{\leq k}) since t−1≥kt-1\geq k. Therefore Δt=ht−ht−1=0\Delta_{t}=h_{t}-h_{t-1}=0 almost surely, which implies It=𝔼⁡[Δt2]=0I_{t}=\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{t}^{2}]=0.

(i) ⇒\Rightarrow (ii): Assume It=0I_{t}=0 for all t>kt>k. Since It=𝔼⁡[Δt2]I_{t}=\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{t}^{2}] and Δt2≥0\Delta_{t}^{2}\geq 0, we have Δt=0\Delta_{t}=0 almost surely for all t>kt>k.

We proceed by backward induction. For t=Tt=T: ΔT=0\Delta_{T}=0 a.s. implies hT=hT−1h_{T}=h_{T-1} a.s. Continuing down to t=k+1t=k+1:

hT=hT−1=⋯=hk+1=hka.s.h_{T}=h_{T-1}=\cdots=h_{k+1}=h_{k}\quad\text{a.s.} (27)

Since hT​(y)=𝔼⁡[Harm⁡(y)∣y]=Harm⁡(y)h_{T}(y)=\mathbb{E}[\Harm(y)\mid y]=\Harm(y), we have Harm⁡(y)=hk​(y≤k)\Harm(y)=h_{k}(y_{\leq k}) almost surely. Setting g:=hkg:=h_{k} completes the proof. ∎

Theorem 10 (Zero Gradient Beyond Horizon).

Under either equivalent condition of Theorem 9, for all t>kt>k:

𝔼y<t​[Covyt|y<t⁡(ht​(y≤t)​∇θ​log⁡Pθ​(yt∣y<t))]=0,\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}}\left[\Cov_{y_{t}\mid y_{<t}}\Big(h_{t}(y_{\leq t})\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})\Big)\right]=0, (28)

and hence position tt contributes nothing to ∇θ𝔼​[Harm⁡(y)]\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}[\Harm(y)].

Proof.

If It=0I_{t}=0, then Var⁡(ht∣y<t)=0\Var(h_{t}\mid y_{<t})=0 almost surely, since It=𝔼⁡[Var⁡(ht∣y<t)]I_{t}=\mathbb{E}[\Var(h_{t}\mid y_{<t})] and variance is non-negative. A random variable with zero conditional variance is almost surely constant given the conditioning. Thus ht​(y≤t)h_{t}(y_{\leq t}) does not depend on yty_{t} given y<ty_{<t}, so the covariance with any function of yty_{t} is zero. ∎

Remark 3 (Why Alignment is Shallow).

Theorem 10 explains why standard alignment produces shallow models. If harm is typically determined by early tokens (e.g. whether the response begins with a refusal) then:

  1. 1.

    Positions beyond the harm horizon receive zero gradient.

  2. 2.

    Alignment pressure concentrates on early positions.

  3. 3.

    Later positions remain at the base model distribution.

This is optimal behavior given the objective as there is no signal to align later positions.

7 Gradient Magnitude Scales with Harm Information

Even when harm is not sharply determined by an early prefix, positions with low harm information receive weak gradient signal. We now make this precise.

Definition 11 (Conditional Fisher Information).

The Fisher information at position tt, conditional on prefix y<ty_{<t}, is:

Ft​(y<t,θ)\displaystyle F_{t}(y_{<t};\theta) :=𝔼yt|y<t[∇θlogPθ(yt∣y<t)\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{y_{t}\mid y_{<t}}\Big[\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t}) (29)
⋅∇θlogPθ(yt∣y<t)⊤]\displaystyle\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})^{\top}\Big]

We write F¯t​(θ):=𝔼y<t​[Ft​(y<t,θ)]\bar{F}_{t}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}}[F_{t}(y_{<t};\theta)] for the marginalized Fisher information.

Lemma 12 (Pointwise Cauchy-Schwarz Bound).

For any fixed prefix y<ty_{<t}, let Ct​(y<t):=Covyt|y<t⁡(ht,∇θ​log​Pθ​(yt∣y<t))C_{t}(y_{<t}):=\Cov_{y_{t}\mid y_{<t}}(h_{t},\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})). Then:

‖Ct​(y<t)‖2≤Varyt|y<t⁡(ht)⋅tr​(Ft​(y<t,θ))\left\|C_{t}(y_{<t})\right\|^{2}\leq\Var_{y_{t}\mid y_{<t}}(h_{t})\cdot\text{tr}(F_{t}(y_{<t};\theta)) (30)
Proof.

By Cauchy-Schwarz applied to each coordinate:

|Cov⁡(ht,st(j))|2≤Var⁡(ht)⋅Var⁡(st(j))\left|\Cov(h_{t},s_{t}^{(j)})\right|^{2}\leq\Var(h_{t})\cdot\Var(s_{t}^{(j)}) (31)

where st(j)=∂θjlog⁡Pθ​(yt∣y<t)s_{t}^{(j)}=\partial_{\theta_{j}}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t}). Summing over coordinates jj:

∑j|Cov⁡(ht,st(j))|2\displaystyle\sum_{j}\left|\Cov(h_{t},s_{t}^{(j)})\right|^{2} ≤Var⁡(ht)⋅∑jVar⁡(st(j))\displaystyle\leq\Var(h_{t})\cdot\sum_{j}\Var(s_{t}^{(j)}) (32)
=Var⁡(ht)⋅tr​(Ft​(y<t))\displaystyle=\Var(h_{t})\cdot\text{tr}(F_{t}(y_{<t}))

where the last equality uses 𝔼⁡[st(j)]=0\mathbb{E}[s_{t}^{(j)}]=0 (the score has zero mean). ∎

Theorem 13 (Gradient Bound).

The gradient contribution from position tt satisfies:

‖Gt​(θ)‖2≤𝔼y<t​[Varyt|y<t⁡(ht)⋅tr​(Ft​(y<t,θ))]\left\|G_{t}(\theta)\right\|^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}}\left[\Var_{y_{t}\mid y_{<t}}(h_{t})\cdot\text{tr}(F_{t}(y_{<t};\theta))\right] (33)

where Gt​(θ):=𝔼y<t​[Ct​(y<t)]G_{t}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}}[C_{t}(y_{<t})] is the gradient contribution defined in Theorem 8.

In particular, if the Fisher information is uniformly bounded by tr​(Ft​(y<t))≤F¯\text{tr}(F_{t}(y_{<t}))\leq\bar{F} for all prefixes, then:

‖Gt​(θ)‖2≤It⋅F¯\left\|G_{t}(\theta)\right\|^{2}\leq I_{t}\cdot\bar{F} (34)
Proof.

By Jensen’s inequality (since ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|^{2} is convex):

‖Gt‖2=‖𝔼y<t​[Ct​(y<t)]‖2≤𝔼y<t​[‖Ct​(y<t)‖2]\|G_{t}\|^{2}=\left\|\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}}[C_{t}(y_{<t})]\right\|^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}}\left[\|C_{t}(y_{<t})\|^{2}\right] (35)

Applying Lemma 12 to each term in the expectation:

≤𝔼y<t​[Varyt|y<t⁡(ht)⋅tr​(Ft​(y<t))]\leq\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}}\left[\Var_{y_{t}\mid y_{<t}}(h_{t})\cdot\text{tr}(F_{t}(y_{<t}))\right] (36)

For the second claim, if tr​(Ft​(y<t))≤F¯\text{tr}(F_{t}(y_{<t}))\leq\bar{F} uniformly:

≤F¯⋅𝔼y<t​[Varyt|y<t⁡(ht)]=F¯⋅It\leq\bar{F}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}}\left[\Var_{y_{t}\mid y_{<t}}(h_{t})\right]=\bar{F}\cdot I_{t} (37)

∎

Remark 4 (Qualitative Conclusion).

The key insight is that ‖Gt‖=O⁡(It)\|G_{t}\|=O(\sqrt{I_{t}}): gradient magnitude scales with the square root of harm information. Positions where It≈0I_{t}\approx 0 receive negligible gradient signal, regardless of the Fisher information. This provides a smooth interpolation between the sharp case (Theorem 10, where It=0I_{t}=0 exactly) and the general case.

Remark 5 (Tightness).

The pointwise bound (Lemma 12) is tight when the score is proportional to the harm innovation:

∇θ​log​Pθ​(yt∣y<t)∝ht​(y≤t)−𝔼⁡[ht∣y<t]\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})\propto h_{t}(y_{\leq t})-\mathbb{E}[h_{t}\mid y_{<t}] (38)

The bound in Theorem 13 may be loose due to Jensen’s inequality if Ct​(y<t)C_{t}(y_{<t}) varies in direction across different prefixes.

8 Equilibrium Analysis

We now characterize the equilibrium of the alignment objective (2).

Theorem 14 (Equilibrium Characterization).

Assume the alignment objective ℋ(θ)=λ𝔼[Harm(y)]+DKL(Pθ∥Pbase)\mathcal{H}(\theta)=\lambda\mathbb{E}[\Harm(y)]+D_{\KL}(P_{\theta}\|P_{\text{base}}) is minimized at θ∗\theta^{*}, and that Pθ∗P_{\theta^{*}} is in an exponential family with the Fisher information matrix F¯t\bar{F}_{t} positive definite at the base model. Then for small λ\lambda, the per-position KL divergence satisfies:

DKL(t)​(θ∗)\displaystyle D_{\KL}^{(t)}(\theta^{*}) :=𝔼y<t[DKL(Pθ∗(⋅∣y<t)∥Pbase(⋅∣y<t))]\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}}\left[D_{\KL}(P_{\theta^{*}}(\cdot\mid y_{<t})\|P_{\text{base}}(\cdot\mid y_{<t}))\right] (39)
=O⁡(λ2​It)\displaystyle=O(\lambda^{2}I_{t})
Proof.

At a local minimum, the first-order condition for position tt is:

λ​Gt​(θ∗)+∇θDKL(t)​(θ∗)=0\lambda G_{t}(\theta^{*})+\nabla_{\theta}D_{\KL}^{(t)}(\theta^{*})=0 (40)

For an exponential family, the KL divergence from the base model satisfies DKL(t)​(θ)=12​(θ−θbase)⊤​F¯t​(θ−θbase)+O⁡(‖θ−θbase‖3)D_{\KL}^{(t)}(\theta)=\frac{1}{2}(\theta-\theta_{\text{base}})^{\top}\bar{F}_{t}(\theta-\theta_{\text{base}})+O(\|\theta-\theta_{\text{base}}\|^{3}) near θbase\theta_{\text{base}}. The gradient is ∇θDKL(t)=F¯t​(θ−θbase)+O⁡(‖θ−θbase‖2)\nabla_{\theta}D_{\KL}^{(t)}=\bar{F}_{t}(\theta-\theta_{\text{base}})+O(\|\theta-\theta_{\text{base}}\|^{2}).

For small λ\lambda, we have θ∗=θbase+O⁡(λ)\theta^{*}=\theta_{\text{base}}+O(\lambda). Substituting into the first-order condition and solving to leading order:

θ∗−θbase=−λ​F¯t−1​Gt​(θbase)+O⁡(λ2)\theta^{*}-\theta_{\text{base}}=-\lambda\bar{F}_{t}^{-1}G_{t}(\theta_{\text{base}})+O(\lambda^{2}) (41)

Thus:

DKL(t)​(θ∗)=λ22​Gt⊤​F¯t−1​Gt+O⁡(λ3)D_{\KL}^{(t)}(\theta^{*})=\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}G_{t}^{\top}\bar{F}_{t}^{-1}G_{t}+O(\lambda^{3}) (42)

By Theorem 13, ‖Gt‖2≤F¯⋅It\|G_{t}\|^{2}\leq\bar{F}\cdot I_{t} when the Fisher information is bounded, so DKL(t)=O⁡(λ2​It)D_{\KL}^{(t)}=O(\lambda^{2}I_{t}). ∎

Corollary 15 (KL Tracks Harm Information).

Positions with It≈0I_{t}\approx 0 have DKL(t)≈0D_{\KL}^{(t)}\approx 0: they remain close to the base model.

This provides theoretical grounding for the empirical observation of Qi et al. (2025) that the KL divergence profile mirrors the harm information profile.

9 Deep Alignment via Recovery Penalties

We established that standard objectives cannot produce deep alignment when harm has a short horizon. To achieve depth, we modify the objective to create gradient signal at all positions. We introduce the deep alignment objective, derive an exact equilibrium characterization paralleling Theorem 14, and prove quantitative robustness guarantees against prefilling attacks.

Definition 16 (Recovery Tokens and Failure).

Let ℛ⊂𝒱\mathcal{R}\subset\mathcal{V} be a set of recovery tokens tokens whose presence at position tt indicates the model is attempting to redirect toward safe behavior (e.g. tokens encoding “I”, “Sorry”, “I cannot”). The recovery failure at position tt is Failt⁡(θ,y<t):=1−Pθ​(yt∈ℛ∣y<t)\Fail_{t}(\theta,y_{<t}):=1-P_{\theta}(y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}\mid y_{<t}).

Definition 17 (Deep Alignment Objective).

The deep alignment objective is:

ℋdeep​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\text{deep}}(\theta) =λ​𝔼y∼Pθ​[Harm⁡(y)]\displaystyle=\lambda\mathbb{E}_{y\sim P_{\theta}}[\Harm(y)] (43)
+μ​𝔼y∼Q​[∑t=1Tγt−1​Failt⁡(θ,y<t)]\displaystyle+\mu\mathbb{E}_{y\sim Q}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma^{t-1}\Fail_{t}(\theta,y_{<t})\right]
+DKL(Pθ∥Pbase)\displaystyle+D_{\KL}(P_{\theta}\|P_{\text{base}})

where QQ is an adversarial prefix distribution, γ∈(0,1]\gamma\in(0,1] is a discount factor, and μ>0\mu>0 controls recovery penalty strength.

Definition 18 (Recovery Information).

The recovery information at position tt is

Jt​(θ):=𝔼y<t∼Q​[pt​(1−pt)],J_{t}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim Q}\big[p_{t}(1-p_{t})\big], (44)

where pt:=Pθ​(yt∈ℛ∣y<t)p_{t}:=P_{\theta}(y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}\mid y_{<t}). This is the analogue of harm information ItI_{t} for the recovery penalty: it measures how much the choice of yty_{t} affects recovery.

The recovery penalty has the same covariance-with-score structure as the harm gradient in Theorem 8. Define the recovery gradient G~t(θ):=−𝔼y<t∼Q[Covyt|y<t(𝟏[yt∈ℛ],∇θlogPθ(yt∣y<t))]\tilde{G}_{t}(\theta):=-\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim Q}[\Cov_{y_{t}\mid y_{<t}}(\mathbf{1}[y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}],\,\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t}))]. The Cauchy–Schwarz machinery of Section 7 transfers directly: ‖G~t‖2≤F¯⋅Jt\|\tilde{G}_{t}\|^{2}\leq\bar{F}\cdot J_{t} (see Appendix Appendix B for the precise bound).

9.1 Deep Equilibrium Characterization

Theorem 19 (Deep Equilibrium).

Under the same assumptions as Theorem 14, for small λ\lambda and μ\mu the minimizer θ∗\theta^{*} of ℋdeep\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{deep}} satisfies:

DKL(t)​(θ∗)=12​‖λ​Gt+μ​γt−1​G~t‖F¯t−12+O⁡((λ+μ)3),D_{\KL}^{(t)}(\theta^{*})=\frac{1}{2}\left\|\lambda G_{t}+\mu\gamma^{t-1}\tilde{G}_{t}\right\|_{\bar{F}_{t}^{-1}}^{2}+O\big((\lambda+\mu)^{3}\big), (45)

where ‖v‖M2:=v⊤​M​v\|v\|_{M}^{2}:=v^{\top}Mv. In particular:

  1. (i)

    For t>kt>k (beyond the harm horizon), Gt=0G_{t}=0 by Theorem 10, so

    DKL(t)​(θ∗)=μ2​γ2​(t−1)2​‖G~t‖F¯t−12+O⁡(μ3).D_{\KL}^{(t)}(\theta^{*})=\frac{\mu^{2}\gamma^{2(t-1)}}{2}\|\tilde{G}_{t}\|_{\bar{F}_{t}^{-1}}^{2}+O(\mu^{3}). (46)

    This is generically positive wherever QQ has support and Jt>0J_{t}>0.

  2. (ii)

    Setting μ=0\mu=0 recovers DKL(t)=O⁡(λ2​It)D_{\KL}^{(t)}=O(\lambda^{2}I_{t}) from Theorem 14.

Proof sketch.

The recovery gradient ∇θRt​(θ)=G~t​(θ)\nabla_{\theta}R_{t}(\theta)=\tilde{G}_{t}(\theta) follows from the same score-function identity used in Theorem 8, since QQ does not depend on θ\theta. With decoupled parameters, the first-order condition at position tt becomes λ​Gt+μ​γt−1​G~t+F¯t​(θ∗−θbase)=0\lambda G_{t}+\mu\gamma^{t-1}\tilde{G}_{t}+\bar{F}_{t}(\theta^{*}-\theta_{\mathrm{base}})=0 to leading order. Solving and substituting into the quadratic KL expansion yields (45). The full proof is in App. Appendix B. ∎

The discount factor γ\gamma controls the depth profile: γ=1\gamma=1 produces uniform recovery KL across positions, while γ<1\gamma<1 induces geometric decay γ2​(t−1)\gamma^{2(t-1)}. The total recovery KL beyond the horizon scales as O⁡(μ2/(1−γ2))O(\mu^{2}/(1-\gamma^{2})), diverging as γ→1\gamma\to 1—formalizing the tradeoff between alignment depth and capability preservation.

9.2 Exact Recovery Probability and Robustness

The perturbative analysis above requires small μ\mu. For positions beyond the harm horizon, the deep objective admits an exact solution in distribution space.

Theorem 20 (Exact Recovery Probability).

For a fixed prefix y<ty_{<t} with t>kt>k, let p0:=Pbase​(yt∈ℛ∣y<t)p_{0}:=P_{\mathrm{base}}(y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}\mid y_{<t}) and β:=μ​γt−1\beta:=\mu\gamma^{t-1}. The optimal conditional distribution is the Gibbs measure

P∗(yt∣y<t)∝Pbase(yt∣y<t)exp(β⋅𝟏[yt∈ℛ]),P^{*}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})\propto P_{\mathrm{base}}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})\exp\big(\beta\cdot\mathbf{1}[y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}]\big), (47)

with optimal recovery probability and KL cost:

P∗​(ℛ∣y<t)\displaystyle P^{*}(\mathcal{R}\mid y_{<t}) =σ⁡(logit⁡(p0)+β),\displaystyle=\sigma\big(\operatorname{logit}(p_{0})+\beta\big), (48)
DKL(P∗∥Pbase)\displaystyle D_{\KL}(P^{*}\|P_{\mathrm{base}}) =β​P∗​(ℛ∣y<t)−log⁡Z,\displaystyle=\beta\,P^{*}(\mathcal{R}\mid y_{<t})-\log Z, (49)

where Z=(1−p0)+p0​eβZ=(1-p_{0})+p_{0}e^{\beta} and σ⁡(x)=(1+e−x)−1\sigma(x)=(1+e^{-x})^{-1}.

Proof sketch.

Beyond the harm horizon, Gt=0G_{t}=0 and the deep objective decouples across prefixes into independent KL-penalized linear problems. Standard variational calculus yields the Gibbs form; the sigmoid and KL expressions follow by direct computation. See App. Appendix B. ∎

The key insight of (48) is that the recovery penalty acts as an additive shift of β\beta in the log-odds of recovery. This enables a clean robustness guarantee.

Definition 21 (Recoverability).

A model PθP_{\theta} is (Q,ϵ)(Q,\epsilon)-recoverable at depth TT if Pθ​(yt∈ℛ∣y<t)≥ϵP_{\theta}(y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}\mid y_{<t})\geq\epsilon for all 1≤t≤T1\leq t\leq T and QQ-almost all prefixes y<ty_{<t}.

Theorem 22 (Robustness Guarantee).

Suppose Pbase​(yt∈ℛ∣y<t)≥pmin>0P_{\mathrm{base}}(y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}\mid y_{<t})\geq p_{\min}>0 for all tt and QQ-almost all prefixes. Then the minimizer of ℋdeep\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{deep}} (beyond the harm horizon) is (Q,ϵ∗)(Q,\epsilon^{*})-recoverable at depth TT, where

ϵ∗=σ⁡(logit⁡(pmin)+μ​γT−1).\epsilon^{*}=\sigma\big(\operatorname{logit}(p_{\min})+\mu\gamma^{T-1}\big). (50)

The total KL cost of recovery beyond the horizon satisfies

∑t=k+1TDKL(t)​(θ∗)\displaystyle\sum_{t=k+1}^{T}D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(t)}(\theta^{*}) ≤∑t=k+1Tμ​γt−1−\displaystyle\leq\sum_{t=k+1}^{T}\mu\gamma^{t-1}-
∑t=k+1Tlog⁡((1−pmin)+pmin​eμ​γt−1)\displaystyle\sum_{t=k+1}^{T}\log\bigl((1-p_{\min})+p_{\min}e^{\mu\gamma^{t-1}}\bigr) (51)
Proof sketch.

The sigmoid form (48) is monotone in p0p_{0}, so the worst case is p0=pminp_{0}=p_{\min}. The worst position is t=Tt=T (where γt−1\gamma^{t-1} is smallest). The KL bound follows from P∗​(ℛ)≤1P^{*}(\mathcal{R})\leq 1 and monotonicity of ZZ in p0p_{0}. The full proof is in Appendix B. ∎

Corollary 23 (Prefilling Attack Resistance).

Under standard alignment, for t>kt>k the model has no additional recovery capability beyond PbaseP_{\mathrm{base}}. Under deep alignment, recovery probability is at least ϵ∗>pmin\epsilon^{*}>p_{\min} at every position. For γ<1\gamma<1, the minimum attack prefix length needed to suppress recovery below δ\delta is

tattack​(δ)=1+log⁡μ−log⁡(logit⁡(δ)−logit⁡(pmin))log⁡(1/γ),t_{\mathrm{attack}}(\delta)=1+\frac{\log\mu-\log(\operatorname{logit}(\delta)-\operatorname{logit}(p_{\min}))}{\log(1/\gamma)}, (52)

which grows logarithmically in μ\mu. For γ=1\gamma=1 and μ≥logit⁡(δ)−logit⁡(pmin)\mu\geq\operatorname{logit}(\delta)-\operatorname{logit}(p_{\min}), no finite prefix suffices.

10 Discussion

10.1 Implications for Alignment Practice

Our main result is that shallow alignment is not a training failure under this formalization as it is the optimal solution to standard objectives when harm has a short horizon. The gradient characterization (Theorem 8) shows that alignment pressure naturally concentrates where harm is determined. This reframes the problem as that achieving deep alignment requires objective modification, not better optimization or more data.

Deeper alignment requires more total KL divergence from the base model. Our equilibrium characterization shows DKL(t)=O⁡(λ2​It)D_{\KL}^{(t)}=O(\lambda^{2}I_{t}): to maintain alignment at position tt, we must pay a KL cost proportional to the harm information there. Expanding ItI_{t} to later positions (via recovery penalties) thus increases total divergence. This suggests a tradeoff between alignment depth and capability preservation as deep alignment may sacrifice some fluency or knowledge by forcing the model further from its base distribution.

Standard alignment evaluations test whether models refuse harmful prompts at the start of generation. Our analysis suggests this is insufficient. A model may appear aligned under such tests while remaining vulnerable to prefilling attacks. Robust evaluation should measure recovery probability P⁡(yt∈ℛ∣y<tharmful)P(y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}\mid y_{<t}^{\text{harmful}}) at multiple positions, not just initial refusal rates.

10.2 Connection to Adversarial Robustness

Our formalization can explain the success of prefilling attacks (Andriushchenko et al., 2024). An attacker who supplies tokens covering the harm horizon bypasses all positions with It>0I_{t}>0. The model then continues from a region where it received no alignment training. This is not a failure of training but a limitation as there was no gradient signal to learn recovery behavior.

An attacker with knowledge of the harm information profile can craft minimal prefilling attacks by supplying just enough tokens to cover the high-ItI_{t} region. Our Cauchy-Schwarz bound (Theorem 13) suggests that gradient magnitude decays with It\sqrt{I_{t}}, so attackers should target the “cliff edge” where ItI_{t} drops to near-zero.

Our deep alignment objective (Definition 17) hypothetically provides a defense by creating Iteff>0I_{t}^{\text{eff}}>0 at all positions, we ensure the model receives training signal for recovery even from deep in a harmful sequence. This is more robust than input filtering, which can be evaded, or adversarial training, which only addresses seen attacks.

10.3 Connection to Representation Engineering

Circuit breakers (Zou et al., 2024) and representation engineering (Zou et al., 2025) operate on internal activations rather than output distributions. Our framework applies to output-level alignment (RLHF, DPO) and does not directly characterize these methods. However, we conjecture a connection. If harmful representations activate at specific layers, the “representation horizon” may relate to our harm horizon. Investigating this connection is an important direction for future work.

Arditi et al. (2024) show that refusal behavior is mediated by a single direction in activation space. This suggests refusal is a “shallow” feature that can be manipulated independently of deeper representations. Our recovery penalty encourages refusal-like behavior at all positions, potentially strengthening this direction throughout the model’s computation.

11 Conclusion

We have provided a gradient-theoretic analysis for why safety alignment in LLMs is shallow under the current popular training methods. The martingale structure of sequence-level harm implies that gradient signal cannot propagate beyond the harm horizon. Standard alignment objectives are therefore incapable of producing deep alignment, regardless of optimization quality. Our deep alignment objective, based on recovery penalties at all positions, offers a principled path to robust safety. We hope this theoretical framework guides future work on alignment techniques that are truly deep.

Limitations

We now discuss the limitations of our work. These limitations suggest important directions for future work and caveats for interpreting our results.

We analyze gradients with respect to output distributions Pθ​(yt|y<t)P_{\theta}(y_{t}|y_{<t}). Representation-level interventions such as circuit breakers and activation steering operate on internal model states and may achieve alignment depth through mechanisms we do not capture. Formalizing the connection between “representation depth” and our “output depth” requires a theory of how internal representations map to output distributions.

We treat Harm⁡(y)\Harm(y) as fixed and known. In practice, harm is estimated by a reward model trained on finite preference data, which may have its own harm horizon as an artifact of training, may produce spurious gradient signal through estimation errors, and may be unreliable on adversarial inputs due to distribution shift. Our theory characterizes alignment to the reward model’s notion of harm, which may diverge from true harm.

Our analysis conditions on a fixed prompt xx. Different prompts induce different harm information profiles It​(x)I_{t}(x), and a model may be deeply aligned for training prompts but shallowly aligned for novel ones. We provide no aggregation principle for combining It​(x)I_{t}(x) across prompts into a single measure of alignment depth.

The deep alignment objective assumes recovery is desirable at all positions, but mid-sequence refusal may sometimes be worse than completing the response and providing context. The feasibility of recovery is formalized by the pmin>0p_{\min}>0 condition in Theorem 22: when the base model assigns negligible probability to recovery tokens, the required penalty μ\mu grows as log⁡(1/pmin)\log(1/p_{\min}), which may be impractically large deep into harmful sequences.

Zero gradient beyond the harm horizon characterizes where training pressure is applied, not where behavior changes. The base model may already be safe (or harmful) at later positions independently of alignment. Our robustness guarantee (Theorem 22) partially closes this gap by characterizing recovery probabilities directly, but only for the deep objective. The standard objective remains characterized only through KL.

Our formalism operates at the token level, but harm is a semantic property. The harm horizon in token space may not correspond to the semantic horizon, as a model might commit to harmful content early but realize it through varied token paths. A semantic-level theory would be more fundamental but remains open.

The equilibrium characterization describes the fixed point of optimization, not the path to it. The exact variational solution (Theorem 20) removes the small-λ\lambda and exponential family assumptions of the perturbative analysis, but assumes unrestricted optimization over per-position distributions, which finite training with early stopping may not achieve.

Transformers have finite capacity and may lack the expressiveness to implement recovery from arbitrary harmful prefixes. The Gibbs solution (Theorem 20) specifies what the optimal conditional distribution looks like, but whether a finite-capacity transformer can approximate it across the diversity of harmful prefixes is an open question.

Finally, our analysis covers single-turn generation. Multi-turn conversations allow recovery across turns. For example, refusing in turn n+1n+1 after partially complying in turn nn and introduce harm horizons that span multiple exchanges, requiring a theory of inter-turn credit assignment that we do not provide.

Appendix A Relaxing the Exponential Family Assumption

Theorem 14 assumes an exponential family parameterization, which provides per-position natural parameters and decouples positions in the first-order optimality condition. Transformers share parameters θ\theta across all positions. We show that the quadratic KL expansion holds for any smooth parameterization, but that shared parameters introduce cross-position coupling that changes the equilibrium characterization in a theoretically informative way.

A.1 General Quadratic Expansion

Lemma 24 (Fisher–Hessian Identity).

For any smoothly parameterized family Pθ​(yt∣y<t)P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t}), the Hessian of the per-position KL divergence at θ=θbase\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{base}} equals the Fisher information:

∂2DKL(t)​(θ)∂θi​∂θj|θbase=F¯t​(θbase)i​j,\frac{\partial^{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(t)}(\theta)}{\partial\theta_{i}\,\partial\theta_{j}}\bigg|_{\theta_{\mathrm{base}}}=\bar{F}_{t}(\theta_{\mathrm{base}})_{ij}, (53)

where F¯t​(θ)=𝔼y<t​[Ft​(y<t,θ)]\bar{F}_{t}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}}\!\bigl[F_{t}(y_{<t};\theta)\bigr] is the marginalized Fisher information (Definition 11).

Proof.

Write DKL(t)(θ)=𝔼y<t[KL(Pθ(⋅∣y<t)∥Pbase(⋅∣y<t))]D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(t)}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}}\!\bigl[\mathrm{KL}(P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid y_{<t})\,\|\,P_{\mathrm{base}}(\cdot\mid y_{<t}))\bigr]. At θ=θbase\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{base}}, DKL(t)=0D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(t)}=0 and ∇θDKL(t)=0\nabla_{\theta}D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(t)}=0 (the base model is a stationary point of the KL from itself). For the Hessian, we use the standard identity. For any two distributions in the same smoothly parameterized family,

∂2∂θi​∂θjKL(Pθ∥Pθ0)|θ=θ0\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\theta_{i}\,\partial\theta_{j}}\mathrm{KL}(P_{\theta}\|P_{\theta_{0}})\bigg|_{\theta=\theta_{0}}
=𝔼y∼Pθ0​[∂log⁡Pθ​(y)∂θi⋅∂log⁡Pθ​(y)∂θj]θ=θ0\displaystyle\quad=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim P_{\theta_{0}}}\!\left[\frac{\partial\log P_{\theta}(y)}{\partial\theta_{i}}\cdot\frac{\partial\log P_{\theta}(y)}{\partial\theta_{j}}\right]_{\theta=\theta_{0}} (54)

which is the Fisher information matrix at θ0\theta_{0}. This holds for any smooth parameterization; the exponential family is not required. Marginalizing over y<ty_{<t} gives the result. ∎

It follows that for any smooth parameterization, the per-position KL admits the expansion

DKL(t)​(θ)\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(t)}(\theta) =12​(θ−θbase)⊤​F¯t​(θbase)​(θ−θbase)\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}(\theta-\theta_{\mathrm{base}})^{\top}\bar{F}_{t}(\theta_{\mathrm{base}})(\theta-\theta_{\mathrm{base}})
+O⁡(‖θ−θbase‖3).\displaystyle\quad+O(\|\theta-\theta_{\mathrm{base}}\|^{3}). (55)

The exponential family assumption in Theorem 14 can therefore be replaced by:

Assumption 1 (Smooth Parameterization).

Pθ​(yt∣y<t)P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t}) is twice continuously differentiable in θ\theta for all yt,y<ty_{t},y_{<t}, and F¯t​(θbase)\bar{F}_{t}(\theta_{\mathrm{base}}) is positive definite.

This is satisfied by transformers with softmax output layers.

A.2 Shared-Parameter Coupling

With shared parameters, the alignment objective is

ℋ⁡(θ)=λ​𝔼​[Harm⁡(y)]+∑t=1TDKL(t)​(θ),\mathcal{H}(\theta)=\lambda\,\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Harm}(y)]+\sum_{t=1}^{T}D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(t)}(\theta),

and the first-order condition is a single equation over all positions:

λ​∑t=1TGt​(θ∗)+∑t=1T∇θDKL(t)​(θ∗)=0.\lambda\sum_{t=1}^{T}G_{t}(\theta^{*})+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\nabla_{\theta}D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(t)}(\theta^{*})=0. (56)

Substituting the quadratic expansion (55):

Proposition 25 (Shared-Parameter Equilibrium).

Under Assumption 1, for small λ\lambda the optimal parameter shift is

θ∗−θbase=−λF¯tot−1∑t=1TGt(θbase)+O(λ2),\theta^{*}-\theta_{\mathrm{base}}=-\lambda\,\bar{F}_{\mathrm{tot}}^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}G_{t}(\theta_{\mathrm{base}})+O(\lambda^{2}), (57)

where F¯tot=∑t=1TF¯t​(θbase)\bar{F}_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bar{F}_{t}(\theta_{\mathrm{base}}) is the total Fisher information.

Proof.

Expanding ∇θDKL(t)​(θ)=F¯t​(θbase)​(θ−θbase)+O⁡(‖θ−θbase‖2)\nabla_{\theta}D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(t)}(\theta)=\bar{F}_{t}(\theta_{\mathrm{base}})(\theta-\theta_{\mathrm{base}})+O(\|\theta-\theta_{\mathrm{base}}\|^{2}) and substituting into (56):

λ​∑tGt+F¯tot​(θ∗−θbase)+O⁡(‖θ∗−θbase‖2)=0.\lambda\sum_{t}G_{t}+\bar{F}_{\mathrm{tot}}(\theta^{*}-\theta_{\mathrm{base}})+O(\|\theta^{*}-\theta_{\mathrm{base}}\|^{2})=0.

Since θ∗=θbase+O⁡(λ)\theta^{*}=\theta_{\mathrm{base}}+O(\lambda), the higher-order terms are O⁡(λ2)O(\lambda^{2}), and solving to leading order gives (57). ∎

The per-position KL divergence at equilibrium is then:

DKL(t)​(θ∗)\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(t)}(\theta^{*}) =λ22​(∑sGs)⊤​F¯tot−1​F¯t​F¯tot−1​(∑sGs)\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}\left(\sum_{s}G_{s}\right)^{\top}\bar{F}_{\mathrm{tot}}^{-1}\,\bar{F}_{t}\,\bar{F}_{\mathrm{tot}}^{-1}\left(\sum_{s}G_{s}\right)
+O⁡(λ3).\displaystyle\quad+O(\lambda^{3}). (58)

A.3 Comparison to the Decoupled Case

In the exponential family setting, per-position natural parameters decouple the first-order condition into TT independent equations, each yielding DKL(t)=O⁡(λ2​ℐt)D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(t)}=O(\lambda^{2}\mathcal{I}_{t}). The shared-parameter expression (58) differs in two ways.

Cross-position dependence.

Even if ℐt=0\mathcal{I}_{t}=0 (so Gt=0G_{t}=0), the per-position KL DKL(t)​(θ∗)D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(t)}(\theta^{*}) can be nonzero. The parameter shift Δ​θ=θ∗−θbase\Delta\theta=\theta^{*}-\theta_{\mathrm{base}} is driven by gradients from all positions; through shared weights, it perturbs the output distribution at every position, including those beyond the harm horizon.

Incidental vs. functional change.

We can decompose the per-position KL into two components:

DKL(t)​(θ∗)\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(t)}(\theta^{*}) =λ22​Gt⊤​F¯tot−1​F¯t​F¯tot−1​Gt⏟functional: driven by local ℐt+\displaystyle=\underbrace{\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}G_{t}^{\top}\bar{F}_{\mathrm{tot}}^{-1}\bar{F}_{t}\,\bar{F}_{\mathrm{tot}}^{-1}G_{t}}_{\text{functional: driven by local }\mathcal{I}_{t}}+
λ22​∑s≠tGs⊤​F¯tot−1​F¯t​F¯tot−1​Gs+cross terms⏟incidental: driven by remote ℐs\displaystyle\underbrace{\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}\sum_{s\neq t}G_{s}^{\top}\bar{F}_{\mathrm{tot}}^{-1}\bar{F}_{t}\,\bar{F}_{\mathrm{tot}}^{-1}G_{s}+\text{cross terms}}_{\text{incidental: driven by remote }\mathcal{I}_{s}} (59)

The functional component vanishes when ℐt=0\mathcal{I}_{t}=0 (by Theorem 8). The incidental component does not; it reflects changes to the position-tt output distribution caused by parameter shifts optimizing other positions.

Proposition 26 (Incidental Change is Safety-Irrelevant).

Let t>kt>k where kk is the harm horizon (Theorem 9). The incidental change at position tt satisfies:

𝔼y<t[Covyt|y<t(ht(y≤t),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}}\!\Bigl[\mathrm{Cov}_{y_{t}\mid y_{<t}}\!\bigl(h_{t}(y_{\leq t}),
log⁡Pθ∗​(yt∣y<t)\displaystyle\qquad\log P_{\theta^{*}}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})
−logPbase(yt∣y<t))]\displaystyle\qquad-\log P_{\mathrm{base}}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})\bigr)\Bigr]
=0.\displaystyle\quad=0. (60)

That is, the distributional change at position tt is uncorrelated with expected harm.

Proof.

Since t>kt>k, harm is determined by y≤ky_{\leq k} (Theorem 9), so ht​(y≤t)=hk​(y≤k)h_{t}(y_{\leq t})=h_{k}(y_{\leq k}) almost surely. This is constant given y<ty_{<t} (since t>kt>k implies y≤k⊆y<ty_{\leq k}\subseteq y_{<t}). A random variable that is constant given the conditioning has zero covariance with any function of yty_{t}. ∎

A.4 Refined Equilibrium Characterization

Combining these observations, we obtain:

Theorem 27 (Shared-Parameter Equilibrium).

Under Assumption 1, for small λ\lambda:

  1. 1.

    For all positions tt:   DKL(t)​(θ∗)=O⁡(λ2​‖F¯tot−1​∑sGs‖F¯t2)D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(t)}(\theta^{*})=O\!\left(\lambda^{2}\left\|\bar{F}_{\mathrm{tot}}^{-1}\sum_{s}G_{s}\right\|_{\bar{F}_{t}}^{2}\right).

  2. 2.

    For positions tt beyond the harm horizon DKL(t)​(θ∗)D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(t)}(\theta^{*}) may be nonzero, but the distributional change is uncorrelated with harm (Proposition 26).

  3. 3.

    If per-position parameters decouple (as in the exponential family case), this reduces to DKL(t)​(θ∗)=O⁡(λ2​ℐt)D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(t)}(\theta^{*})=O(\lambda^{2}\mathcal{I}_{t}), recovering Theorem 14.

The qualitative conclusion of the main body is preserved but refined. Standard alignment changes late-position behavior incidentally, through the coupling of shared parameters, but these changes carry no safety-relevant information. Deep alignment, namely the distributional change that is functionally related to harm, remains confined to the harm horizon.

The shared-parameter analysis generates a prediction that distinguishes it from the decoupled theory. For aligned models with shared parameters, positions tt beyond the harm horizon satisfy DKL(t)​(θ∗)>0D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(t)}(\theta^{*})>0 but Pθ∗​(yt∈R∣y<tharmful)≈Pbase​(yt∈R∣y<tharmful)P_{\theta^{*}}(y_{t}\in R\mid y_{<t}^{\mathrm{harmful}})\approx P_{\mathrm{base}}(y_{t}\in R\mid y_{<t}^{\mathrm{harmful}}). That is, the aligned model’s output distribution differs from the base model at late positions, but this difference does not manifest as increased recovery capability.

The decoupled theory predicts DKL(t)≈0D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(t)}\approx 0 for t>kt>k. The shared-parameter theory predicts nonzero KL that is safety-irrelevant. Measuring both DKL(t)D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(t)} and recovery probability P⁡(yt∈R∣y<tharmful)P(y_{t}\in R\mid y_{<t}^{\mathrm{harmful}}) across positions would distinguish the two accounts and, more practically, would test whether nonzero late-position KL should be interpreted as evidence of deep alignment (it should not).

Appendix B Proofs and Supplementary Results for Deep Alignment

This appendix provides full proofs for the results in Section 9 and additional remarks on their scope.

B.1 Recovery Gradient Bound

Lemma 28 (Recovery Gradient Bound).

The recovery gradient G~t(θ):=−𝔼y<t∼Q[Covyt|y<t(𝟏[yt∈ℛ],∇θlogPθ(yt∣y<t))]\tilde{G}_{t}(\theta):=-\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim Q}[\Cov_{y_{t}\mid y_{<t}}(\mathbf{1}[y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}],\,\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t}))] satisfies

‖G~t​(θ)‖2≤𝔼y<t∼Q​[tr⁡(Ft​(y<t,θ))]⋅Jt​(θ).\|\tilde{G}_{t}(\theta)\|^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim Q}\big[\mathrm{tr}(F_{t}(y_{<t};\theta))\big]\cdot J_{t}(\theta). (61)

If tr⁡(Ft​(y<t,θ))≤F¯\mathrm{tr}(F_{t}(y_{<t};\theta))\leq\bar{F} uniformly, then ‖G~t‖2≤F¯⋅Jt\|\tilde{G}_{t}\|^{2}\leq\bar{F}\cdot J_{t}.

Proof.

The argument is identical in structure to the proof of Theorem 13. Write st(j)=∂θjlog⁡Pθ​(yt∣y<t)s_{t}^{(j)}=\partial_{\theta_{j}}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t}). For a fixed prefix y<ty_{<t}, by Cauchy–Schwarz applied coordinate-wise:

|Covyt|y<t(𝟏[yt∈ℛ],st(j))|2\displaystyle\left|\mathrm{Cov}_{y_{t}|y_{<t}}\!\left(\mathbf{1}[y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}],\,s_{t}^{(j)}\right)\right|^{2}
≤Varyt|y<t(𝟏[yt∈ℛ])\displaystyle\quad\leq\mathrm{Var}_{y_{t}|y_{<t}}\!\left(\mathbf{1}[y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}]\right)
⋅Varyt|y<t​(st(j)).\displaystyle\quad\cdot\mathrm{Var}_{y_{t}|y_{<t}}\!\left(s_{t}^{(j)}\right). (62)

Summing over coordinates jj and using Var⁡(st(j))=𝔼⁡[(st(j))2]\Var(s_{t}^{(j)})=\mathbb{E}[(s_{t}^{(j)})^{2}] (since 𝔼⁡[st(j)]=0\mathbb{E}[s_{t}^{(j)}]=0):

‖Covyt|y<t(𝟏[yt∈ℛ],∇θlogPθ)‖2\displaystyle\left\|\mathrm{Cov}_{y_{t}|y_{<t}}\!\left(\mathbf{1}[y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}],\,\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}\right)\right\|^{2}
≤pt​(1−pt)⋅tr⁡(Ft​(y<t,θ)).\displaystyle\quad\leq p_{t}(1-p_{t})\cdot\mathrm{tr}\!\left(F_{t}(y_{<t};\theta)\right). (63)

where pt=Pθ​(yt∈ℛ∣y<t)p_{t}=P_{\theta}(y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}\mid y_{<t}). Taking the outer expectation over y<t∼Qy_{<t}\sim Q and applying Jensen’s inequality (‖𝔼⁡[X]‖2≤𝔼⁡[‖X‖2]\|\mathbb{E}[X]\|^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}[\|X\|^{2}]):

‖G~t‖2\displaystyle\|\tilde{G}_{t}\|^{2} ≤𝔼y<t∼Q​[pt​(1−pt)⋅tr⁡(Ft​(y<t,θ))]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim Q}\big[p_{t}(1-p_{t})\cdot\mathrm{tr}(F_{t}(y_{<t};\theta))\big] (64)
≤𝔼y<t∼Q​[tr⁡(Ft​(y<t,θ))]⋅Jt​(θ).\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim Q}\big[\mathrm{tr}(F_{t}(y_{<t};\theta))\big]\cdot J_{t}(\theta). (65)

The second inequality uses the uniform bound on the Fisher trace. ∎

B.2 Proof of Theorem 19

Full proof of Theorem 19.

The deep alignment objective decomposes as

ℋdeep​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{deep}}(\theta) =λ​𝔼Pθ​[Harm⁡(y)]\displaystyle=\lambda\,\mathbb{E}_{P_{\theta}}[\mathrm{Harm}(y)]
+μ∑t=1Tγt−1Rt(θ)\displaystyle\quad+\mu\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma^{t-1}R_{t}(\theta)
+∑t=1TDKL(t)(θ),\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{t=1}^{T}D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(t)}(\theta), (66)

where Rt​(θ):=𝔼y<t∼Q​[Failt​(θ,y<t)]R_{t}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim Q}[\mathrm{Fail}_{t}(\theta,y_{<t})].

Recovery gradient identification.

Since QQ does not depend on θ\theta:

∇θRt​(θ)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}R_{t}(\theta)
=−𝔼y<t∼Q​[∇θPθ​(yt∈ℛ∣y<t)]\displaystyle\quad=-\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim Q}\!\left[\nabla_{\theta}P_{\theta}(y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}\mid y_{<t})\right]
=−𝔼y<t∼Q​[∑r∈ℛPθ​(r∣y<t)​∇θ​log⁡Pθ​(r∣y<t)]\displaystyle\quad=-\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim Q}\!\left[\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}P_{\theta}(r\mid y_{<t})\,\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(r\mid y_{<t})\right]
=−𝔼y<t∼Q[𝔼yt|y<t[𝟏[yt∈ℛ]\displaystyle\quad=-\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim Q}\!\Big[\mathbb{E}_{y_{t}\mid y_{<t}}\!\big[\mathbf{1}[y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}]
⋅∇θlogPθ(yt∣y<t)]].\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})\big]\Big]. (67)

Since 𝔼yt|y<t​[∇θ​log​Pθ​(yt∣y<t)]=0\mathbb{E}_{y_{t}\mid y_{<t}}[\nabla_{\theta}\log P_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})]=0, this equals G~t​(θ)\tilde{G}_{t}(\theta) from Definition 18.

Perturbative expansion.

With decoupled per-position parameters, the first-order condition at position tt is

λ​Gt​(θ∗)+μ​γt−1​G~t​(θ∗)+∇θDKL(t)​(θ∗)=0.\lambda\,G_{t}(\theta^{*})+\mu\gamma^{t-1}\tilde{G}_{t}(\theta^{*})+\nabla_{\theta}D_{\KL}^{(t)}(\theta^{*})=0. (68)

Using the quadratic KL expansion (Lemma 24):

∇θDKL(t)​(θ)=F¯t​(θ−θbase)+O⁡(‖θ−θbase‖2).\nabla_{\theta}D_{\KL}^{(t)}(\theta)=\bar{F}_{t}(\theta-\theta_{\mathrm{base}})+O(\|\theta-\theta_{\mathrm{base}}\|^{2}).

Since θ∗=θbase+O⁡(λ+μ)\theta^{*}=\theta_{\mathrm{base}}+O(\lambda+\mu), we evaluate GtG_{t} and G~t\tilde{G}_{t} at θbase\theta_{\mathrm{base}} up to higher-order corrections. Solving (68) to leading order:

θ∗−θbase=−F¯t−1​(λ​Gt+μ​γt−1​G~t)+O⁡((λ+μ)2),\theta^{*}-\theta_{\mathrm{base}}=-\bar{F}_{t}^{-1}\big(\lambda\,G_{t}+\mu\gamma^{t-1}\tilde{G}_{t}\big)+O\big((\lambda+\mu)^{2}\big), (69)

where GtG_{t} and G~t\tilde{G}_{t} are evaluated at θbase\theta_{\mathrm{base}}. Substituting into DKL(t)​(θ∗)=12​(θ∗−θbase)⊤​F¯t​(θ∗−θbase)+O⁡((λ+μ)3)D_{\KL}^{(t)}(\theta^{*})=\frac{1}{2}(\theta^{*}-\theta_{\mathrm{base}})^{\top}\bar{F}_{t}(\theta^{*}-\theta_{\mathrm{base}})+O((\lambda+\mu)^{3}):

DKL(t)​(θ∗)=12​‖λ​Gt+μ​γt−1​G~t‖F¯t−12+O⁡((λ+μ)3).D_{\KL}^{(t)}(\theta^{*})=\frac{1}{2}\big\|\lambda G_{t}+\mu\gamma^{t-1}\tilde{G}_{t}\big\|_{\bar{F}_{t}^{-1}}^{2}+O\big((\lambda+\mu)^{3}\big). (70)

Cases.

For t>kt>k: It=0I_{t}=0 implies Gt=0G_{t}=0 by Theorem 10, so DKL(t)=μ2​γ2​(t−1)2​‖G~t‖F¯t−12+O⁡(μ3)D_{\KL}^{(t)}=\frac{\mu^{2}\gamma^{2(t-1)}}{2}\|\tilde{G}_{t}\|_{\bar{F}_{t}^{-1}}^{2}+O(\mu^{3}). For μ=0\mu=0: the recovery terms vanish, reducing to λ22​‖Gt‖F¯t−12+O⁡(λ3)=O⁡(λ2​It)\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}\|G_{t}\|_{\bar{F}_{t}^{-1}}^{2}+O(\lambda^{3})=O(\lambda^{2}I_{t}) by Lemmas 28 and 13. ∎

Remark 6 (Aggregate recovery KL).

For γ<1\gamma<1, the total recovery KL beyond the horizon satisfies

∑t>kDKL(t)​(θ∗)=O⁡(μ21−γ2),\sum_{t>k}D_{\KL}^{(t)}(\theta^{*})=O\!\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{1-\gamma^{2}}\right), (71)

assuming ‖G~t‖F¯t−12\|\tilde{G}_{t}\|_{\bar{F}_{t}^{-1}}^{2} is bounded uniformly in tt. This diverges as γ→1\gamma\to 1, formalizing the depth–capability tradeoff: uniform-depth alignment (γ=1\gamma=1) requires unbounded total KL divergence from the base model.

Remark 7 (Non-degeneracy of recovery gradient).

The recovery information Jt>0J_{t}>0 whenever there exists a prefix y<ty_{<t} in the support of QQ with 0<Pθ​(yt∈ℛ∣y<t)<10<P_{\theta}(y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}\mid y_{<t})<1. By Lemma 28, this is necessary for G~t≠0\tilde{G}_{t}\neq 0. It is also generically sufficient: G~t=0\tilde{G}_{t}=0 despite Jt>0J_{t}>0 would require the score function to be orthogonal to the recovery indicator conditional on every prefix, which is a non-generic condition of measure zero in parameter space.

B.3 Proof of Theorem 20

Full proof of Theorem 20.

For t>kt>k, the harm gradient Gt=0G_{t}=0 and the deep objective’s contribution at prefix y<ty_{<t} reduces to the pointwise problem

minP∈Δ⁡(𝒱)β(1−P(ℛ))+DKL(P∥P0),\min_{P\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})}\;\beta\big(1-P(\mathcal{R})\big)+D_{\KL}(P\|P_{0}), (72)

where β=μ​γt−1\beta=\mu\gamma^{t-1}, P0=Pbase(⋅∣y<t)P_{0}=P_{\mathrm{base}}(\cdot\mid y_{<t}), and Δ⁡(𝒱)\Delta(\mathcal{V}) is the probability simplex.

Introducing a Lagrange multiplier ν\nu for the constraint ∑ytP⁡(yt)=1\sum_{y_{t}}P(y_{t})=1:

∂∂P⁡(yt)[\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial P(y_{t})}\Bigg[ ∑ytP⁡(yt)​log⁡P⁡(yt)P0​(yt)\displaystyle\sum_{y_{t}}P(y_{t})\log\frac{P(y_{t})}{P_{0}(y_{t})}
−β∑ytP(yt)𝟏[yt∈ℛ]\displaystyle-\beta\sum_{y_{t}}P(y_{t})\mathbf{1}[y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}]
−ν(∑P−1)]=0.\displaystyle-\nu\Big(\sum P-1\Big)\Bigg]=0. (73)

This gives logP∗​(yt)P0​(yt)+1−β 1[yt∈ℛ]−ν=0\log\frac{P^{*}(y_{t})}{P_{0}(y_{t})}+1-\beta\,\mathbf{1}[y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}]-\nu=0, so

P∗(yt)=P0(yt)exp(β 1[yt∈ℛ]+ν−1).P^{*}(y_{t})=P_{0}(y_{t})\exp\big(\beta\,\mathbf{1}[y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}]+\nu-1\big). (74)

The normalization constraint determines eν−1=1/Ze^{\nu-1}=1/Z where

Z=∑ytP0(yt)exp(β 1[yt∈ℛ])=(1−p0)+p0eβ.Z=\sum_{y_{t}}P_{0}(y_{t})\exp\big(\beta\,\mathbf{1}[y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}]\big)=(1-p_{0})+p_{0}e^{\beta}. (75)

Strict convexity of the KL divergence ensures this is the unique global minimizer.

Recovery probability:

∎

Remark 8 (Interpretation).

The recovery penalty acts as an additive shift of β\beta in log-odds space. A base probability of p0=0.01p_{0}=0.01 is boosted much more in absolute terms than p0=0.5p_{0}=0.5 for the same β\beta, since the sigmoid is steepest near 1/21/2. Crucially, the mechanism requires p0>0p_{0}>0: if the base model assigns zero probability to all recovery tokens for a given prefix, no finite β\beta can create recovery.

Remark 9 (Importance weighting).

The recovery term in ℋdeep\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{deep}} samples prefixes from QQ while the KL term averages over PθP_{\theta}. In the non-parametric optimization, the pointwise subproblem at prefix y<ty_{<t} becomes

minP(⋅|y<t)\displaystyle\min_{P(\cdot|y_{<t})}\; q⁡(y<t)pθ​(y<t)​μ​γt−1​(1−P⁡(ℛ))\displaystyle\frac{q(y_{<t})}{p_{\theta}(y_{<t})}\,\mu\gamma^{t-1}(1-P(\mathcal{R}))
+DKL(P∥Pbase(⋅|y<t)),\displaystyle+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|P_{\mathrm{base}}(\cdot|y_{<t})), (79)

where the density ratio q/pθq/p_{\theta} acts as an importance weight. The Gibbs solution retains the form of Theorem 20 with β\beta replaced by β~t​(y<t):=μ​γt−1⋅q⁡(y<t)/pθ​(y<t)\tilde{\beta}_{t}(y_{<t}):=\mu\gamma^{t-1}\cdot q(y_{<t})/p_{\theta}(y_{<t}). For harmful prefixes that the aligned model avoids but QQ upweights, β~t≫βt\tilde{\beta}_{t}\gg\beta_{t}, amplifying recovery pressure precisely where it is most needed.

B.5 Within-Horizon Recovery

Proposition 29 (Within-Horizon Solution).

For t≤kt\leq k, the non-parametric solution to ℋdeep\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{deep}} takes the form

P∗​(yt∣y<t)\displaystyle P^{*}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t}) ∝Pbase​(yt∣y<t)\displaystyle\propto P_{\mathrm{base}}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})
⋅exp⁡(−λ​ht​(y≤t)CLOSE\displaystyle\cdot\exp\!\Big(-\lambda\,h_{t}(y_{\leq t})
+μγt−1𝟏[yt∈ℛ]).\displaystyle\qquad+\mu\gamma^{t-1}\mathbf{1}[y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}]\Big). (84)

The harm tilt −λ​ht-\lambda\,h_{t} reduces probability of tokens leading to high expected harm, while the recovery tilt +μγt−1𝟏[⋅∈ℛ]+\mu\gamma^{t-1}\mathbf{1}[\cdot\in\mathcal{R}] boosts recovery tokens. When these align (recovery tokens have low hth_{t}), the effects reinforce; when they conflict (a recovery token would increase expected harm, e.g. by producing an incoherent refusal), the two terms compete, with the tradeoff governed by λ/μ\lambda/\mu.

Proof.

For t≤kt\leq k, the per-prefix subproblem includes both the harm and recovery terms. The Lagrangian for the variational problem has two tilts: −λ​ht​(y≤t)-\lambda h_{t}(y_{\leq t}) from the harm objective and +μγt−1𝟏[yt∈ℛ]+\mu\gamma^{t-1}\mathbf{1}[y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}] from the recovery penalty. The KL-penalized optimization with a linear objective ∑ici​P​(yt=i)\sum_{i}c_{i}P(y_{t}=i) has the well-known Gibbs solution P∗​(yt)∝P0​(yt)​exp⁡(cyt)P^{*}(y_{t})\propto P_{0}(y_{t})\exp(c_{y_{t}}). Combining both linear terms gives the result. Note that ht​(y≤t)h_{t}(y_{\leq t}) depends on yty_{t} (unlike the beyond-horizon case), so this is not a simple indicator tilt. ∎

B.6 The pmin>0p_{\min}>0 Assumption

Remark 10 (Softmax models).

Condition Pbase​(yt∈ℛ∣y<t)≥pmin>0P_{\mathrm{base}}(y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}\mid y_{<t})\geq p_{\min}>0 is automatically satisfied by any model with a softmax output layer and finite logits, since softmax assigns strictly positive probability to every token. However, pminp_{\min} may be exponentially small for prefixes deep into harmful content. If pmin=e−Lp_{\min}=e^{-L} for some L>0L>0, achieving ϵ∗≥1/2\epsilon^{*}\geq 1/2 requires μ​γT−1≥L\mu\gamma^{T-1}\geq L: the penalty must overcome the base model’s log-odds against recovery. For a base model that assigns pmin=10−6p_{\min}=10^{-6} to recovery tokens after a long harmful prefix, this means μ​γT−1≥6​ln⁡10≈13.8\mu\gamma^{T-1}\geq 6\ln 10\approx 13.8, which is achievable but requires a substantial penalty that will also incur substantial KL cost.
